scenes.title: LEAD()
scenes.narration: LEAD lets a row peek forward to access the value of a following row within its partition, without any self-join.

scenes.title: How LEAD() Works
bullets: Returns a value from a row that comes after the current one
Offset defaults to 1 — the very next row
Default value is returned when no following row exists
scenes.narration: LEAD returns a value from a row that appears after the current row in the ordered partition. Its signature takes the column to read, an optional offset, and an optional default. The offset defaults to one, meaning the very next row. When there is no following row, such as at the end of a partition, LEAD returns the default you supply or null.

scenes.title: Finding the Next Order Date
scenes.code:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  order_date,
  LEAD(order_date, 1) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id
    ORDER BY order_date
  ) AS next_order_date
FROM orders;
scenes.narration: This query partitions orders by customer and sorts them by date. LEAD of order_date with an offset of one pulls each customer's next order date onto the current row. For a customer's most recent order there is no following row, so next_order_date comes back null. This immediately reveals the gap between consecutive purchases without joining the table to itself.

scenes.title: Period-Over-Period Change
scenes.code:
SELECT
  month,
  revenue,
  LEAD(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS next_revenue,
  LEAD(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) - revenue AS change_to_next
FROM monthly_revenue;
scenes.narration: Here we order monthly revenue by month and use LEAD to bring the following month's revenue onto each row. By subtracting the current revenue from the next month's revenue, we compute the change heading into the next period. Because the offset defaults to one, we simply write LEAD of revenue without specifying it. The final month has no successor, so its change value is null.

scenes.title: LEAD() vs LAG()

left.title: LEAD()
points: Looks forward to a following row
Ideal for next-event and forecasting deltas

right.title: LAG()
points: Looks backward to a preceding row

scenes.narration: LEAD and LAG are mirror images. LEAD looks forward to a following row and answers what comes next, which suits next-event lookups. LAG looks backward to a preceding row and answers what came before, which suits previous-period comparisons. They share the same signature and differ only in direction.

scenes.text: Always specify ORDER BY inside OVER — LEAD is meaningless without it, and provide a sensible default so boundary rows don't silently become NULL.
scenes.narration: Never omit the ORDER BY inside OVER, because LEAD has no meaning without a defined order, and supply a default so boundary rows are handled cleanly.
